# 1. SpatialExperiment ---------------------------------------------------------

In keeping with interoperability, we use the `SpatialExperiment` object from the `SpatialExperiment` package as the central linking framework across many of the packages.

``` {r Environement setup}
# Check if renv is installed, if not install it
if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("renv")
}

# Load renv
library(renv)

# Setup project environment (renv configuration, directories, temp paths)
# This script is located at MAIN/PROG/Scripts/setup_project.R
source("MAIN/PROG/Scripts/setup_project.R")

# Run project setup
# Set auto_snapshot = TRUE to automatically update renv.lock when packages differ
dirs <- setup_project(
  root_dir = "/mnt/b/Projects/Image_Analysis_Projects/SJ_04.2/MAIN",
  auto_snapshot = TRUE, # Set to TRUE for automatic lockfile updates
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

## 1.1 Creating a SpatialExperiment object -------------------------------------

The vignette for the `SpatialExperiment` package explains how to turn a matrix or data.frame into a `SpatialExperiment`.

If you have a `.csv` file or a `.xlsx` file, this can be read into R using `read_csv()` and `read_xlsx()` from the `readxl` package and converted into a matrix or data.frame. You could also use `read.csv()` or `read.delim()` in base R.

If you have a `Seurat` object, you can convert this to a `SingleCellExperiment` using the `as.SingleCellExperiment()` function or back again using `as.Seurat()`.

A `SpatialExperiment` object is very similar to a `SingleCellExperiment` but with spatial coordinates stored in the `spatialCoords()` slot. Many people analyse spatial data using a `SingleCellExperiment` object with the spatial coordinates stored in `colData`. Most of our packages are accepting of this approach.

For visualisations, we recommend duplicating your `spatialCoords()` in the `reducedDim()` slot and in the `colData`.

## 1.2 Setting global parameters -----------------------------------------------

The code below automatically detects the number of available CPU cores on your system and configures parallel processing accordingly. If you’re on a Windows machine, it uses a socket-based backend (SnowParam), while Unix-based systems (macOS/Linux) use a fork-based backend (MulticoreParam).

If only one core is available or parallel execution is disabled, it defaults to serial processing. We recommend using at least 2 cores as parts of the workflow can be computationally intensive. If you do not wish to use multiple cores, you can set use_mc = FALSE.

``` {r global_parameters}
# Install ggplot2 if not already installed--------------------------------------
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  message("  Installing ggplot2...")
  BiocManager::install("ggplot2", ask = FALSE, update = FALSE)
}
# Load ggplot2
library(ggplot2)


# Set global parameters---------------------------------------------------------
# Set the default theme to classic
theme_set(theme_classic())
options(
  # Show 10 rows and 8 columns instead of the default 10 rows and 5 columns
  # when printing data frames
  dplyr.print_min = 10,
  dplyr.print_max = 8,
  # Use knitr for chunk output
  knitr.table.format = "html"
)

# Extract directory paths from setup--------------------------------------------
ROOT_DIR <- dirs$ROOT_DIR
RES_DIR <- dirs$RES_DIR
# ── v2: redirect output to RESv2 ──
RES_DIR <- file.path(ROOT_DIR, "RESv2")
dir.create(RES_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
CHECKPOINT_SUFFIX <- "_v2"
PROG_DIR <- dirs$PROG_DIR
CONFIG_DIR <- dirs$CONFIG_DIR
TEMP_DIR <- dirs$TEMP_DIR

# set seed for reproducibility--------------------------------------------------
set.seed(51773)

# Configure parallel processing-------------------------------------------------
# Load parallel configuration script
source(file.path(PROG_DIR, "Scripts", "configure_parallel_processing.R"))

# Configure parallelization-----------------------------------------------------
#
# n_cores options:
#   "serial" - No parallelization (safest, slowest)
#   "max"    - Use all available cores (fastest but may impact system)
#   <number> - Specify exact number of cores (e.g., 8, 16)
#
# mode options:
#   "socket" - Socket-based parallelization (Java-compatible, default)
#   "fork"   - Fork-based parallelization (Unix only, NOT compatible with Java!)
#
# Examples:
#   config <- configure_parallel_processing(n_cores = "serial")
#   config <- configure_parallel_processing(n_cores = "max", mode = "socket")
#   config <- configure_parallel_processing(n_cores = 8, mode = "socket")
#   config <- configure_parallel_processing(n_cores = 16, mode = "fork", for_java = FALSE)

config <- configure_parallel_processing(
  n_cores = 48, # Options: "serial", "max", or a number (e.g., 9)
  mode = "fork", # Options: "socket" (Java-compatible) or "fork" (faster, no Java)
  for_java = TRUE, # Keep TRUE for Java/RBioFormats compatibility
  verbose = TRUE # Show configuration details
)

# Extract BPPARAM and n_cores for use in the workflow-----------------------
BPPARAM <- config$BPPARAM
nCores <- config$n_cores

# Configure Java and RBioFormats for OME-TIFF processing---------------------
# This script handles:
#   - Java configuration and initialization
#   - rJava installation and setup
#   - RBioFormats installation
#   - Bio-Formats JAR file management
#   - Verification of complete setup
source(file.path(PROG_DIR, "Scripts", "setup_java_rbioformats.R"))

# Run setup and capture status-------------------------------------------------
java_setup_status <- setup_java_rbioformats()

# Set global variables for downstream use-------------------------------------
java_available <- java_setup_status$java_available
rbioformats_available <- java_setup_status$rbioformats_available
```

# 2. Cell segmentation and pre-processing

The segmentation pipeline has been upgraded to use **Cellpose v4 (CP-SAM)** on the GPU, reading directly from the original pyramidal OME-TIFF files. This approach eliminates the need for splitting the image into individual channel TIFFs, preserving full **float32** precision and significantly reducing processing time.

## 2.1 Python Pipeline Configuration

The pipeline is implemented in `segment_and_quantify.py`. It performs channel discovery (via OME-XML), nuclear segmentation, adaptive enhancement, and quantification in a single pass.

``` {r python_pipeline_setup}
# 1. Pipeline Paths-------------------------------------------------------------
image_name <- "EGFR_TREG_2" # Options: "CAR_TREG_1", "CAR_TREG_2", "EGFR_TREG_1", "EGFR_TREG_2"
pathToImages <- file.path(dirname(ROOT_DIR), "data", "input")
omeTiffFile <- file.path(pathToImages, paste0(image_name, ".ome.tif"))

# 2. Python Configuration-------------------------------------------------------
python_script <- file.path(PROG_DIR, "Scripts", "segment_and_quantify.py")
# Organised output: PROG/SEGMENTATION/{image_name}/
output_dir <- file.path(PROG_DIR, "SEGMENTATION", image_name)
if (!dir.exists(output_dir)) dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE)

nuclear_marker <- "DNA-Brilliant Violet 421"

# 3. Control Parameters---------------------------------------------------------
run_test_mode <- FALSE # Set to TRUE for 2000x2000 center crop (fast)
use_gpu <- TRUE
cache_enhanced <- FALSE
# Set to TRUE to save/load enhanced channels (fast OME-TIFF re-runs)
sharpen_nuclear <- 0 # Strength of sharpening (0 to disable)
denoise_nuclear <- 0 # Gaussian blur sigma (0 to disable)
tile_norm_blocksize <- 100 # Tile normalization block size (0 to disable, 100 recommended)
export_ome <- TRUE # Set to TRUE to generate the enhanced OME-TIFF (even in test mode)
verbose_logging <- TRUE # Set to TRUE to see detailed Cellpose progress logs

message("--- Pipeline Configuration ---")
message("Image: ", image_name)
message("Source: ", omeTiffFile)
message("Output: ", output_dir)
message("Nuclear marker: ", nuclear_marker)
message("Test mode: ", run_test_mode)
```

## 2.2 Execute Segmentation (Python)

We execute the Python script using a system call. The results (cells.csv, masks.npz, diagnostics.md) will be saved to the image-specific segmentation directory.

``` {r run_python_segmentation}
log_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(image_name, "_pipeline_run.log"))

# Construct CLI arguments
cmd_args <- c(
  "--image-name", image_name,
  "--ome-tiff", omeTiffFile,
  "--nuclear-channel", paste0("\"", nuclear_marker, "\""),
  "--output-dir", output_dir,
  "--log-file", log_file
)

if (use_gpu) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--gpu")
if (run_test_mode) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--test")
if (cache_enhanced) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--cache-enhanced")
if (export_ome) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--export-ome")
if (sharpen_nuclear > 0) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--sharpen-nuclear", sharpen_nuclear)
if (denoise_nuclear > 0) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--denoise-nuclear", denoise_nuclear)
if (tile_norm_blocksize > 0) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--tile-norm-blocksize", tile_norm_blocksize)
if (verbose_logging) cmd_args <- c(cmd_args, "--verbose")

message("\n=== Running Python Segmentation Pipeline ===")
message("Command: python3 ", python_script, " ", paste(cmd_args, collapse = " "))

# Execute
t0 <- Sys.time()
system2("python3", args = c("-u", python_script, cmd_args), stdout = "", stderr = "")
elapsed <- Sys.time() - t0

message("\n✓ Pipeline complete in ", round(as.numeric(elapsed, units = "mins"), 1), " minutes")
```



# 3. Quality Control

Variability in marker intensity across images is a common challenge in spatial imaging, often driven by technical factors like staining efficiency, imaging conditions, or sample preparation. For instance, a marker such as CD3 might appear overly bright in one sample and faint in another, even if the underlying biology is similar. These inconsistencies can blur the distinction between marker-positive and -negative cells, leading to misclassification and unreliable comparisons between and within samples.

Because raw intensities aren't always directly comparable across or within images, quality control is an essential next step after segmentation. The `simpleSeg` package includes tools to support this process, with functions for visualising expression, detecting batch effects, and applying normalisation. These steps help harmonise marker distributions across samples, clarify cell populations, and improve the reliability of downstream analyses.

## 3.2 Marker Density Plots: Assess Batch Effects

Visualize the distribution of all markers across images to assess batch effects.

``` {r marker_density_plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# Generate density plots and statistics
marker_stats <- generate_marker_density_plots(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  res_dir = RES_DIR
)
```

## 3.3 UMAP: Visualize Batch Effects in Reduced Dimensions

Another way to visualize batch effects is by applying dimensionality reduction techniques (like UMAP) to the marker expression data and plotting the cells in two dimensions. If there are no major batch effects, cells from different images should largely overlap or mix well in this reduced space. However, if strong batch effects are present, cells will tend to cluster by image rather than by biological similarity—indicating that technical variation is dominating the structure of the data.

``` {r umap_batch_effects, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Generate UMAP with parallelization (excludes DNA/Isotype markers)
combined_spe <- generate_umap_batch_effects(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  res_dir = RES_DIR,
  exclude_patterns = c("DNA", "Isotype"),
  n_cores = NULL # Auto-detect
)
```

> **Interpretation**: If cells cluster by image (two distinct groups) rather than mixing uniformly, this indicates batch effects. Technical variation between images is driving the separation rather than true biological differences. This suggests normalization may be needed.

## 3.4 Normalize Cell Intensities

If batch effects are present (as indicated by the density plots and UMAP), we can use normalization to correct for image-level technical variation. The `normalize_cells_wrapper()` function applies multiple normalization methods to harmonize marker intensities across images.

### Normalization Parameters:

- **`transformation`**: No arcsinh transformation applied (set to NULL)
- **`methods`**: `c("trim99", "mean", "PC1")` - Trim outliers, mean-center, correct for PC1 variation
- **`exclude_patterns`**: DNA markers excluded from normalization
- **`n_cores`**: Auto-detects available cores for parallel processing

``` {r normalize_cells}
# Normalize cell intensities across images (excludes DNA markers)
combined_spe <- normalize_cells_wrapper(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  exclude_patterns = "DNA",
  methods = c("trim99", "mean", "PC1"),
  n_cores = NULL # Auto-detect
)
```

## 3.5 Post-Normalization QC: Density Plots

Let's check whether normalization has improved the marker distributions using the normalized data.

``` {r post_norm_density_all, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# Generate normalized density plots for all markers
generate_post_norm_density_plots(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  res_dir = RES_DIR
)
```

> **What to look for**: After normalization, the marker distributions should be more consistent across images. Bimodal markers (positive/negative populations) should show clearer separation, and the peaks should align better between images.

Generate a UMAP using the normalized data to see if batch effects have been reduced.

``` {r post_norm_umap, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}

  combined_spe = combined_spe,
```

# 4. Unsupervised Clustering for Cell Annotation

Cell type annotation is the process of assigning each cell a specific identity based on its marker expression profile. Identifying cell types is a key step in many spatial analysis workflows, as it shapes how we analyse tissue composition, measure cell-cell interactions, and track disease mechanisms.

But cell type annotation isn't always clear-cut. Marker expression often varies along a continuum rather than forming distinct groups, and overlapping profiles combined with technical noise can blur boundaries, making it tricky to assign confident labels. These uncertainties can cascade through your analysis, affecting clustering, interpretation, and downstream results.

There are two main ways to assign cell types: **unsupervised clustering** and **supervised annotation**. Clustering groups cells based on similarity in marker expression, which can uncover novel or unexpected populations—but biological expertise is often necessary to interpret and label those clusters. Annotation, on the other hand, leverages reference datasets from well-characterised samples to directly assign cell type labels, improving consistency and reproducibility, though it depends on having a relevant and high-quality reference.

Both approaches come with trade-offs. Clustering can miss subtle or rare populations and is sensitive to parameter choices, such as the number of clusters, which can greatly influence results. Annotation risks misclassifying cells if the reference doesn't capture all the diversity in the sample. This section focuses on **unsupervised clustering**—covering how to select appropriate parameters, determine the optimal number of clusters, and interpret results effectively.

## 4.2 Prepare Data for Clustering

We'll use the normalized data (`norm` assay) for clustering, as it has reduced batch effects while preserving biological variation.

``` {r prepare_clustering_data}
# Load clustering analysis functions
source(file.path(PROG_DIR, "Scripts", "clustering_analysis.R"))

# Create clustering output directory
clustering_dir <- file.path(RES_DIR, "Clustering")
dir.create(clustering_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
message("Clustering outputs will be saved to: ", clustering_dir)

# Get clustering markers (stored as attribute from normalization)
clustering_markers <- attr(combined_spe, "use_markers")

if (is.null(clustering_markers)) {
  # Fallback: exclude DNA and Isotype markers
  all_markers <- rownames(combined_spe)
  clustering_markers <- all_markers[!grepl("DNA|Isotype", all_markers)]
}

message("\nMarkers for clustering: ", length(clustering_markers))
message("  ", paste(clustering_markers, collapse = ", "))

# Verify normalized data is available
if (!"norm" %in% assayNames(combined_spe)) {
  stop("norm assay not found. Please run normalization first (Section 3.4).")
}

message("\n✓ Ready for clustering with ", format(ncol(combined_spe), big.mark = ","), " cells")
```

## 4.3 Estimate Optimal Number of Clusters

Before clustering, it's helpful to estimate how many clusters best represent the structure of your data. We'll use the `estimate_optimal_clusters()` function, which supports both discriminant-based and distance-based methods.

### Methods:
- **Discriminant**: Finds a projection that maximizes separation between clusters
- **Distance-based metrics**:
  - **Gap Statistic**: Compares within-cluster variation to null reference
  - **Jump Statistic**: Measures structural changes when adding clusters
  - **Slope Statistic**: Examines rate of change in clustering quality
  - **Within Cluster Dissimilarity (WCD)**: Quantifies within-cluster similarity
  - **Silhouette**: Combines cohesion and separation measures

``` {r estimate_num_clusters, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
# Estimate optimal k and generate elbow plots
cluster_estimation <- estimate_optimal_clusters(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  clustering_markers = clustering_markers,
  res_dir = RES_DIR,
  kSeq = 5:25, # Range of k values to test
  initial_k = 15, # Initial estimate for FuseSOM
  seed = 51773
)

# Extract results
optimal_k_disc <- cluster_estimation$optimal_k_disc
cluster_estimation$elbow_plot
```

> **How to interpret elbow plots**: Look for the "elbow" point where the metric begins to level off. This suggests that adding more clusters beyond this point gives diminishing returns. The optimal k is typically at or just before this inflection point.

## 4.4 Run FuseSOM Clustering with Optimal K

Based on the cluster estimation results, we'll choose an appropriate number of clusters and run FuseSOM.

``` {r run_fusesom_final}
# Choose optimal k based on the plots
# You can adjust this based on biological expectations
message("\nCluster estimation summary:")
message("  Discriminant method: ", optimal_k_disc)
message("  Review the elbow plots above to select optimal k")

# Choose final k (adjust based on elbow plots)
optimal_k <- 15 # Modify this based on your elbow plots

message("\n✓ Using k = ", optimal_k, " clusters for final clustering")

# Run FuseSOM clustering
combined_spe <- run_fusesom_clustering(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  clustering_markers = clustering_markers,
  optimal_k = optimal_k,
  seed = 51773
)

# Store cluster table for later use
cluster_table <- table(colData(combined_spe)$clusters)
```

## 4.5 Visualize Clustering Results: Marker Heatmaps

Generate both FuseSOM and scater heatmaps to visualize marker expression patterns by cluster.

``` {r cluster_heatmaps, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
# Generate both heatmap types
generate_cluster_heatmaps(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  clustering_markers = clustering_markers,
  res_dir = RES_DIR
)
```

> **Interpreting the heatmap**: Each row represents a cluster, and each column represents a marker. Bright colors (high expression) help identify the marker profile of each cluster. For example:
> - Clusters with high CD4 but low CD8 → CD4+ T cells
> - Clusters with high CD19 → B cells
> - Clusters with high FoxP3 and CD4 → Regulatory T cells

## 4.6.1 Post-Hoc Marker-Based Cell Type Gating

FuseSOM cluster boundaries can shift between runs. To ensure stable identification of key cell populations, we apply deterministic marker-based gates that override the cluster-derived labels for Tfh, Tfr, B Cells, and Activated B Cells.

Thresholds are detected automatically via **KDE valley detection** — finding the local minimum between the negative (near-zero) and positive peaks in each marker's expression distribution.

``` {r posthoc_marker_gating, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# Set to FALSE to use cluster-only annotations (v2 reversion)
APPLY_POST_HOC_GATING <- FALSE

if (APPLY_POST_HOC_GATING) {
message("\n=== Post-Hoc Marker-Based Cell Type Gating ===")

# --- Bimodal Threshold Detection via KDE Valley Finding ---
find_bimodal_threshold <- function(expr, marker_name, min_floor = NULL,
                                    min_peak_ratio = 0.05, sigma_mult = 15,
                                    valley_selection = "rightmost",
                                    force_sigma = FALSE,
                                    kde_adjust = 0.7) {
  # Sharper KDE (lower adjust) resolves shoulders into detectable peaks
  d <- density(expr, n = 512, adjust = kde_adjust)
  dy <- diff(d$y)

  # Find local maxima (peaks) and local minima (valleys)
  peaks <- which(diff(sign(dy)) == -2) + 1
  valleys <- which(diff(sign(dy)) == 2) + 1

  # Require two substantial peaks — second peak must be >= min_peak_ratio of tallest.
  threshold <- NULL
  method <- NULL

  if (!force_sigma && length(peaks) >= 2) {
    max_height <- max(d$y[peaks])
    substantial <- peaks[d$y[peaks] >= min_peak_ratio * max_height]

    if (length(substantial) >= 2) {
      # Find ALL valleys between the outermost substantial peaks
      leftmost_pk <- min(d$x[substantial])
      rightmost_pk <- max(d$x[substantial])
      between <- valleys[d$x[valleys] > leftmost_pk & d$x[valleys] < rightmost_pk]

      if (length(between) > 0) {
        if (valley_selection == "rightmost") {
          best <- between[which.max(d$x[between])]
        } else {
          best <- between[which.min(d$x[between])]
        }
        threshold <- d$x[best]
        method <- paste0("KDE valley (", valley_selection, ")")
      }
    }
  }

  # Fallback for unimodal distributions: place threshold just right of main peak.
  # Estimate the negative peak's spread from its LEFT flank (uncontaminated by
  # positive tail), then set threshold at mode + N*sigma.
  if (is.null(threshold) && length(peaks) >= 1) {
    primary_idx <- peaks[which.max(d$y[peaks])]
    peak_x <- d$x[primary_idx]
    peak_y <- d$y[primary_idx]
    half_max <- peak_y / 2

    # Find left-side half-maximum crossing
    left_side <- which(d$x < peak_x)
    if (length(left_side) > 0) {
      left_hm_idx <- left_side[which.min(abs(d$y[left_side] - half_max))]
      left_half_width <- peak_x - d$x[left_hm_idx]
      # Convert HWHM to sigma: HWHM = sigma * sqrt(2 * ln(2))
      sigma_est <- left_half_width / sqrt(2 * log(2))
      threshold <- peak_x + sigma_mult * sigma_est
      method <- paste0("mode + ", sigma_mult, "\u03C3 (mode=", round(peak_x, 2),
                       ", \u03C3=", round(sigma_est, 2), ")")
    }
  }

  # Last resort fallback
  if (is.null(threshold)) {
    threshold <- unname(quantile(expr, 0.98))
    method <- "98th percentile (last resort)"
  }

  # Enforce minimum floor — clamp threshold upward if below min_floor
  if (!is.null(min_floor) && threshold < min_floor) {
    message("  ", marker_name, ": threshold ", round(threshold, 4),
            " below min_floor ", min_floor, " — clamping upward")
    threshold <- min_floor
    method <- paste0(method, " → clamped to min_floor=", min_floor)
  }

  message("  ", marker_name, ": threshold = ", round(threshold, 4), " [", method, "]")
  list(threshold = threshold, method = method, density = d)
}

# --- Marker-to-Channel Mapping ---
# Note: import_python_results.R strips the "ch_" prefix from channel names
gating_markers <- list(
  CD4          = "CD4-Brilliant Violet 421",
  Foxp3_endo   = "Foxp3-PerCP-Cy5.5",
  GFP          = "GFP-FITC",
  CXCR5        = "CXCR5-PE",
  PD1          = "PD1-Brilliant Violet 421",
  CD19         = "CD19-FITC",
  CD40         = "CD40-PerCP-Cy5.5"
)

# Verify all markers exist in the SPE
available_markers <- rownames(combined_spe)
missing <- setdiff(unlist(gating_markers), available_markers)
if (length(missing) > 0) stop("Missing markers in SPE: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))

# --- Extract Normalized Expression ---
message("\nExtracting normalized expression for gating markers...")
gate_expr <- lapply(gating_markers, function(ch) {
  assay(combined_spe[ch, ], "norm")[1, ]
})

# --- Compute Thresholds ---
# Per-marker overrides:
#   CD4/CD19: leftmost valley (liberal) — disambiguated by mutual exclusivity below
#   Foxp3_endo: high min_peak_ratio forces mode+σ (shoulder is not a real 2nd peak)
message("\nDetecting bimodal thresholds:")
threshold_overrides <- list(
  CD4        = list(valley_selection = "leftmost"),
  CD19       = list(valley_selection = "leftmost"),
  CD40       = list(kde_adjust = 0.3, min_peak_ratio = 0.01, min_floor = 7.0),
  CXCR5      = list(kde_adjust = 0.3),
  GFP        = list(force_sigma = TRUE),
  Foxp3_endo = list(force_sigma = TRUE)
)

gate_thresholds <- list()
gate_results <- list()
for (nm in names(gating_markers)) {
  args <- c(list(expr = gate_expr[[nm]], marker_name = nm),
            threshold_overrides[[nm]])
  result <- do.call(find_bimodal_threshold, args)
  gate_thresholds[[nm]] <- result$threshold
  gate_results[[nm]] <- result
}

# --- Diagnostic Plots ---
message("\nGenerating threshold diagnostic plots...")
diag_dir <- file.path(RES_DIR, "QC_plots", "gating_thresholds")
if (!dir.exists(diag_dir)) dir.create(diag_dir, recursive = TRUE)

for (nm in names(gating_markers)) {
  expr_vals <- gate_expr[[nm]]
  thresh <- gate_thresholds[[nm]]
  d <- gate_results[[nm]]$density
  method <- gate_results[[nm]]$method
  n_pos <- sum(expr_vals > thresh)
  n_neg <- sum(expr_vals <= thresh)

  p_diag <- ggplot(data.frame(x = expr_vals), aes(x = x)) +
    geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4, color = "black") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = thresh, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    annotate("text", x = thresh, y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = -0.1,
             label = paste0("Threshold: ", round(thresh, 3), "\n", method),
             color = "red", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("text", x = min(expr_vals) + 0.1, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
             label = paste0("Negative: ", format(n_neg, big.mark = ",")),
             color = "grey40", size = 3.5) +
    annotate("text", x = max(expr_vals) - 0.1, y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = 1,
             label = paste0("Positive: ", format(n_pos, big.mark = ",")),
             color = "darkgreen", size = 3.5) +
    labs(
      title = paste0("Gating Threshold: ", nm),
      subtitle = paste0("Channel: ", gating_markers[[nm]]),
      x = "Normalized Expression", y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_classic()

  ggsave(file.path(diag_dir, paste0("threshold_", nm, ".png")),
    p_diag, width = 8, height = 5, bg = "white"
  )
}
message("  Diagnostic plots saved to: ", basename(diag_dir), "/")

# --- CD40 Per-Image Diagnostic ---
# Investigate whether the global CD40 threshold sits differently relative to
# each image's distribution (potential source of condition-specific bias).
message("\n--- CD40 Per-Image Gating Diagnostic ---")

cd40_expr <- gate_expr$CD40
cd40_thresh <- gate_thresholds$CD40
image_ids <- combined_spe$imageID

# Step 1: Per-image CD40 density overlay with global threshold
cd40_df <- data.frame(
  expr = cd40_expr,
  imageID = image_ids,
  condition = ifelse(grepl("CAR", image_ids), "CAR-Treg", "EGFR-Treg"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

p_cd40_per_image <- ggplot(cd40_df, aes(x = expr, fill = condition)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cd40_thresh, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = cd40_thresh, y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = -0.1,
           label = paste0("Global: ", round(cd40_thresh, 3)),
           color = "red", size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~imageID, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "CD40 Expression by Image — Global Threshold Overlay",
    subtitle = paste0("Channel: ", gating_markers$CD40,
                      " | Threshold: ", round(cd40_thresh, 3)),
    x = "Normalized Expression", y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p_cd40_per_image)
ggsave(file.path(diag_dir, "threshold_CD40_per_image.png"),
       p_cd40_per_image, width = 10, height = 8, bg = "white")
message("  Saved per-image CD40 density plot")

# Step 2: Per-image gating outcome table (CD19+ breakdown)
cd19_expr <- gate_expr$CD19
cd19_thresh <- gate_thresholds$CD19
cd40_df$cd19_pos <- cd19_expr > cd19_thresh
cd40_df$cd40_pos <- cd40_expr > cd40_thresh

gating_summary <- cd40_df %>%
  filter(cd19_pos) %>%
  group_by(imageID, condition) %>%
  summarise(
    total_cd19_pos = n(),
    activated_b    = sum(cd40_pos),
    regular_b      = sum(!cd40_pos),
    pct_activated  = round(100 * sum(cd40_pos) / n(), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
message("\n  Per-image B Cell gating (CD19+ cells only):")
print(as.data.frame(gating_summary))

# Step 3: Per-image CD40 threshold what-if analysis
message("\n  Per-image CD40 threshold comparison (what-if):")
message("  Global CD40 threshold: ", round(cd40_thresh, 4))

per_image_thresholds <- data.frame(
  imageID = character(), condition = character(),
  global_thresh = numeric(), image_thresh = numeric(),
  global_pct_pos = numeric(), image_pct_pos = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (img in unique(as.character(image_ids))) {
  img_mask <- image_ids == img
  img_expr <- cd40_expr[img_mask]
  img_result <- find_bimodal_threshold(img_expr, marker_name = paste0("CD40 [", img, "]"))
  img_thresh <- img_result$threshold

  n_global_pos <- sum(img_expr > cd40_thresh)
  n_image_pos  <- sum(img_expr > img_thresh)
  n_total      <- length(img_expr)

  per_image_thresholds <- rbind(per_image_thresholds, data.frame(
    imageID         = img,
    condition       = ifelse(grepl("CAR", img), "CAR-Treg", "EGFR-Treg"),
    global_thresh   = round(cd40_thresh, 4),
    image_thresh    = round(img_thresh, 4),
    thresh_diff     = round(img_thresh - cd40_thresh, 4),
    global_pct_pos  = round(100 * n_global_pos / n_total, 1),
    image_pct_pos   = round(100 * n_image_pos / n_total, 1),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}
message("\n  Per-image vs global threshold comparison:")
print(as.data.frame(per_image_thresholds))

# Step 4: CD40 density within B Cell Zone only (post-annotation)
# NOTE: This uses the annotation column which is set AFTER section 7.
# If running section 4 standalone (before section 7), skip this block.
if ("annotation" %in% colnames(colData(combined_spe)) &&
    "B_Cell_Zone" %in% combined_spe$annotation) {
  bcz_mask <- combined_spe$annotation == "B_Cell_Zone"
  bcz_cd40_df <- data.frame(
    expr = cd40_expr[bcz_mask],
    imageID = image_ids[bcz_mask],
    condition = ifelse(grepl("CAR", image_ids[bcz_mask]),
                       "CAR-Treg", "EGFR-Treg"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  p_bcz_cd40 <- ggplot(bcz_cd40_df, aes(x = expr, fill = condition)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = "black") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = cd40_thresh, linetype = "dashed",
               color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~imageID, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
      title = "CD40 Expression in B Cell Zone Only",
      subtitle = paste0("Global threshold: ", round(cd40_thresh, 3),
                        " | Cells in B_Cell_Zone annotation"),
      x = "Normalized Expression", y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  print(p_bcz_cd40)
  ggsave(file.path(diag_dir, "threshold_CD40_B_Cell_Zone.png"),
         p_bcz_cd40, width = 10, height = 8, bg = "white")
  message("  Saved B Cell Zone CD40 density plot")
} else {
  message("  (Skipping B Cell Zone plot — annotation column not yet available)")
}

message("\n--- End CD40 Diagnostic ---\n")

# --- Apply Gating Rules ---
message("\nApplying post-hoc gating rules...")

# Boolean vectors for each marker
is_cd4_pos       <- gate_expr$CD4 > gate_thresholds$CD4
is_foxp3_endo_pos <- gate_expr$Foxp3_endo > gate_thresholds$Foxp3_endo
is_gfp_pos       <- gate_expr$GFP > gate_thresholds$GFP
is_cxcr5_pos     <- gate_expr$CXCR5 > gate_thresholds$CXCR5
is_pd1_pos       <- gate_expr$PD1 > gate_thresholds$PD1
is_cd19_pos      <- gate_expr$CD19 > gate_thresholds$CD19
is_cd40_pos      <- gate_expr$CD40 > gate_thresholds$CD40

# CD4/CD19 mutual exclusivity: these are lineage markers that cannot co-express.
# Liberal thresholds may flag cells as dual-positive — resolve by comparing expression.
dual_pos_idx <- which(is_cd4_pos & is_cd19_pos)
if (length(dual_pos_idx) > 0) {
  cd4_higher <- gate_expr$CD4[dual_pos_idx] >= gate_expr$CD19[dual_pos_idx]
  is_cd4_pos[dual_pos_idx[!cd4_higher]] <- FALSE
  is_cd19_pos[dual_pos_idx[cd4_higher]] <- FALSE
  message("  CD4/CD19 mutual exclusivity: ", format(length(dual_pos_idx), big.mark = ","),
          " dual-positive cells resolved (",
          format(sum(cd4_higher), big.mark = ","), " \u2192 CD4+, ",
          format(sum(!cd4_higher), big.mark = ","), " \u2192 CD19+)")
}
message("  After disambiguation: ",
        format(sum(is_cd4_pos), big.mark = ","), " CD4+, ",
        format(sum(is_cd19_pos), big.mark = ","), " CD19+")

# Composite: FoxP3+ = either endogenous OR transgenic
is_foxp3_pos <- is_foxp3_endo_pos | is_gfp_pos

# Start with FuseSOM-derived labels
# Note: annotate_cell_types() writes to $cell_type; downstream code uses both
# $cell_type (UMAP, spatial plots) and $cellType (spicyR, colocalization)
original_labels <- combined_spe$cell_type
new_labels <- original_labels

# Rule 3: CD19+, CD40- → B Cells
mask_bcell <- is_cd19_pos & !is_cd40_pos
new_labels[mask_bcell] <- "B Cells"

# Rule 4: CD19+, CD40+ → Activated B Cells
mask_act_bcell <- is_cd19_pos & is_cd40_pos
new_labels[mask_act_bcell] <- "Activated B Cells"

# Rule 1: CD4+, FoxP3-, (CXCR5+ OR PD1+) → Tfh
mask_tfh <- is_cd4_pos & !is_foxp3_pos & (is_cxcr5_pos | is_pd1_pos)
new_labels[mask_tfh] <- "T Follicular Helper Cells"

# Rule 2b: CD4+, Foxp3-PerCP+, GFP-, (CXCR5+ OR PD1+) → Endogenous Tfr
mask_tfr_endo <- is_cd4_pos & is_foxp3_endo_pos & !is_gfp_pos & (is_cxcr5_pos | is_pd1_pos)
new_labels[mask_tfr_endo] <- "T Follicular Regulatory (Endogenous)"

# Rule 2a: CD4+, GFP+, (CXCR5+ OR PD1+) → Transgenic Tfr
mask_tfr_trans <- is_cd4_pos & is_gfp_pos & (is_cxcr5_pos | is_pd1_pos)
new_labels[mask_tfr_trans] <- "T Follicular Regulatory (Transgenic)"

# --- Apply to SPE (update both column names for downstream compatibility) ---
combined_spe$cell_type <- new_labels
combined_spe$cellType <- new_labels

# --- Summary ---
changed <- sum(original_labels != new_labels)
message("\nPost-hoc gating reclassified ", format(changed, big.mark = ","), " of ",
        format(ncol(combined_spe), big.mark = ","), " cells (",
        round(changed / ncol(combined_spe) * 100, 1), "%)")

message("\nReclassification breakdown:")
reclassified <- data.frame(
  original = original_labels[original_labels != new_labels],
  new = new_labels[original_labels != new_labels]
)
if (nrow(reclassified) > 0) {
  reclass_summary <- reclassified %>%
    group_by(original, new) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(desc(n))
  print(reclass_summary, n = 20)
}

message("\nFinal cell type distribution:")
print(sort(table(combined_spe$cellType), decreasing = TRUE))

# --- Filter Rare Cell Types (<100 cells) ---
message("\nFiltering rare cell types (fewer than 100 cells)...")
celltype_counts <- table(combined_spe$cell_type)
rare_types <- names(celltype_counts[celltype_counts < 100])

if (length(rare_types) > 0) {
  message("  Removing ", length(rare_types), " rare cell type(s):")
  for (rt in rare_types) {
    message("    - ", rt, " (", celltype_counts[rt], " cells)")
  }

  keep_cells <- !combined_spe$cell_type %in% rare_types
  combined_spe <- combined_spe[, keep_cells]

  # Drop unused factor levels from both annotation columns
  combined_spe$cell_type <- as.character(combined_spe$cell_type)
  combined_spe$cellType <- as.character(combined_spe$cellType)

  # Remove rare types from color mapping
  celltype_colors <- celltype_colors[!names(celltype_colors) %in% rare_types]

  message("  Remaining: ", format(ncol(combined_spe), big.mark = ","), " cells across ",
          length(unique(combined_spe$cell_type)), " cell types")
} else {
  message("  No rare cell types found — all have ≥100 cells")
}

message("\nCell type distribution after rare-type filtering:")
print(sort(table(combined_spe$cellType), decreasing = TRUE))

} else {
  message("\n=== Skipping Post-Hoc Gating (APPLY_POST_HOC_GATING = FALSE) ===")
  message("Using cluster-only annotations from section 4.6")
  message("\nCell type distribution (cluster-only):")
  print(sort(table(combined_spe$cellType), decreasing = TRUE))
}
```

## 4.7.5 Filter Artifact Clusters

Based on visual inspection of the UMAP and spatial plots, some clusters may represent artifacts (e.g., non-specific staining, doublets, or biologically implausible populations). We will remove these before downstream analysis.

Specifically removing:
- **Doublets/Multiplets**: High expression across almost all markers.
- **Low-quality / Artifacts**: High isotype control, negative corrected FoxP3 — non-biological signal.

``` {r}
# Define cell types to remove
artifacts_to_remove <- c(
  "Doublets/Multiplets",
  "Low-quality / Artifacts"
)

# SAFETY CHECK: Ensure data is loaded and has annotations
if (ncol(combined_spe) == 0) {
  stop("Error: 'combined_spe' is empty. Please re-run Section 4.6 (or reload from checkpoint).")
}
if (!"cell_type" %in% colnames(colData(combined_spe))) {
  stop("Error: 'cell_type' column not found. Please run Section 4.6 first.")
}

# Count before removal
n_before <- ncol(combined_spe)

# Filter the object
keep_idx <- !combined_spe$cell_type %in% artifacts_to_remove

# Second safety check: don't let it remove EVERYTHING
if (sum(keep_idx, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
  warning("Warning: Filtering would remove ALL cells. Keeping original object.")
  n_after <- n_before
} else {
  combined_spe <- combined_spe[, keep_idx & !is.na(keep_idx)]
  n_after <- ncol(combined_spe)
}

n_removed <- n_before - n_after

message("✓ Removed ", format(n_removed, big.mark = ","), " cells designated as artifacts.")
message("  Remaining cells: ", format(n_after, big.mark = ","))

# Update cluster table after filtering
cluster_table <- table(colData(combined_spe)$cell_type)

# Regenerate visualizations with cleaned data
message("\nRegenerating visualizations with artifact-free data...")
celltype_viz_clean <- visualize_celltype_umap(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  res_dir = RES_DIR,
  optimal_k = optimal_k,
  celltype_colors = celltype_colors
)

# Display cleaned UMAP
celltype_viz_clean$umap_plot

# Display cleaned spatial plots
for (img_name in names(celltype_viz_clean$spatial_plots)) {
  print(celltype_viz_clean$spatial_plots[[img_name]])
}
```

> **Note**: Removing these cells ensures that downstream spatial statistics (Section 5) are not biased by technical artifacts.

---

> **Common Clustering Issues:**
>
> - **Smearing**: Multiple clusters express the same marker → may need better normalization
> - **Too few clusters**: Markers overlap too much → increase k
> - **Too many clusters**: Tiny clusters with unclear identity → decrease k
> - **Unbalanced clusters**: One huge cluster + many tiny ones → may indicate segmentation or normalization issues

# 5. Cell Localization Between Pairs of Cell Types

Spatial co-localisation analysis helps uncover whether specific cell types are found near each other more (or less) often than expected by chance. This can reveal insights into immune infiltration, tumour-stroma interactions, or the organisation of functional niches.

Before drawing conclusions from co-localisation patterns, it's important to recognise the potential confounding factors that can distort results. Tissue architecture is rarely random—cells are often organised into structured regions, influenced by development, disease states, or sampling. If this spatial inhomogeneity isn't accounted for, standard co-localisation methods can misinterpret natural density variations as meaningful interactions. Similarly, differences in cell abundance across images—due to biology or technical variability—can bias association metrics.

In this section, we demonstrate how to use the **spicyR** package to detect co-localisation patterns while accounting for tissue inhomogeneity and cell abundance—ensuring results that are both statistically sound and biologically meaningful.

## 5.2 Prepare Data for Spatial Analysis

Before running spicyR, we need to ensure our SpatialExperiment object has the correct structure:
- Cluster labels in `colData`
- Image IDs in `colData`
- Spatial coordinates in `spatialCoords()`

``` {r prepare_spatial_data}
# Prepare SpatialExperiment object for spatial analysis
combined_spe <- prepare_spatial_data(combined_spe)

# Store summary variables for later use
n_cells <- ncol(combined_spe)
n_images <- length(unique(combined_spe$imageID))
n_cell_types <- length(unique(combined_spe$cellType))

```

> **Note**: With only 2 images, we cannot perform condition-based comparisons (which require multiple replicates per condition). However, we can still:
> 1. Quantify co-localisation patterns within each image
> 2. Compare co-localisation between the two images
> 3. Visualize spatial relationships

## 5.3 Quantify Cell Type Co-localisation with spicyR

The **L-function** is a statistical tool used to quantify spatial relationships between two cell types—specifically, whether they tend to be closer together (co-localised) or further apart (dispersed) than would be expected by chance.

For each cell of type A, we count how many cells of type B are found within a certain radius. This is done across all A–B cell pairs in the image, and for a range of radii. If the observed number of B cells near A cells is consistently higher than expected under a random (Poisson) null model, it suggests **positive spatial association** (co-localisation). If it's lower, it indicates **negative spatial association** (dispersion).

### 5.3.1 Calculate L-function for All Pairwise Combinations

We'll calculate the L-function for multiple radii to capture both local and global spatial relationships.

``` {r calculate_lfunction, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
# Calculate L-function for all cell type pairs
lfunction_output <- calculate_lfunction(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  coloc_dir = coloc_dir,
  radii = c(20, 50, 100),
  sigma = NULL,
  seed = 51773
)

# Extract results
lfunction_results <- lfunction_output$lfunction_results
```

## 5.4 Compare Co-localisation Between Images

Since we have two images, let's compare the co-localisation patterns between them.

``` {r compare_images, fig.width=14, fig.height=10}
# Compare co-localizations between images
comparison_results <- compare_colocalizations(
  lfunction_results = lfunction_results,
  coloc_dir = coloc_dir
)

# Extract results
lfunction_summary <- comparison_results$lfunction_summary
lfunction_long <- comparison_results$lfunction_long
lfunction_long_export <- comparison_results$lfunction_long_export
top_different_pairs <- comparison_results$top_different_pairs
```

## 5.7 Accounting for Tissue Inhomogeneity

Tissue structure is rarely homogeneous. Dense regions can create apparent co-localisation that isn't biologically meaningful. We can account for this by setting the `sigma` parameter in `getPairwise()`.

``` {r tissue_inhomogeneity, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
# Calculate tissue inhomogeneity corrected L-function
corrected_results <- calculate_inhomogeneity_corrected(
  combined_spe = combined_spe,
  lfunction_results = lfunction_results,
  coloc_dir = coloc_dir,
  sigma = 20,
  radii = c(20, 50, 100)
)

# Extract results
lfunction_corrected <- corrected_results$lfunction_corrected
correction_comparison <- corrected_results$correction_comparison
lfunction_corrected_long <- corrected_results$lfunction_corrected_long
```

> **Sigma Parameter**: Controls how much we smooth out local density variations. Higher sigma = more correction for tissue structure. Typical values: 10-50 pixels depending on image resolution and tissue architecture.

## 5.10 Statistical Comparison with Pseudotiling

Since we have a small number of images, we use a **pseudotiling** strategy to generate pseudo-replicates. This allows us to perform formal statistical testing using `spicyR::spicy()`.

### 5.10.1 Define Conditions and Run Analysis

We first define the treatment conditions (e.g., CAR vs EGFR) based on image names, then run the tiling and colocalization analysis.

``` {r spicy_analysis, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Define conditions in colData
# Map image names to groups (adjust patterns as needed)
combined_spe$condition <- factor(ifelse(
  grepl("CAR", combined_spe$imageID), "CAR", "EGFR"
))

# Run the integrated spicy analysis (includes tiling if needed)
spicy_results <- run_spicy_analysis(
  spe = combined_spe,
  condition_col = "condition",
  subject_col = "imageID",
  radii = 100
)

# Display significance plot
spicyR::signifPlot(spicy_results, breaks = c(-1, 0, 1))
```

> **Interpretation**: 
> - The **Significance Plot** shows cell type pairs that are differentially colocalized between conditions.
> - **Red** indicates higher colocalization in one condition, **Blue** in the other.
> - This analysis uses pseudo-replicates (tiles) to estimate variance and provide p-values.

### 5.10.2 Export Results

``` {r export_spicy}
# Extract statistics using topPairs (handling version/structure differences)
spicy_stats <- as.data.frame(spicyR::topPairs(spicy_results, n = Inf))

# Add cell pair as a readable column
spicy_stats$cell_pair <- paste(spicy_stats$from, spicy_stats$to, sep = " → ")

# Save results
spicy_file <- file.path(coloc_dir, "spicy_colocalization_stats.csv")
write.csv(spicy_stats, spicy_file, row.names = FALSE)

# Save significance plot
png(file.path(coloc_dir, "spicy_significance_plot.png"), width = 10, height = 8, units = "in", res = 300)
spicyR::signifPlot(spicy_results, breaks = c(-1, 0, 1))
dev.off()

message("✓ Spicy colocalization results saved to: ", basename(spicy_file))
```

``` {r verify_spicy_direction}
# Check levels to confirm which group is the 'case'
lvls <- levels(combined_spe$condition)
message("Condition levels: ", paste(lvls, collapse = ", "))
message("Comparison: ", lvls[2], " vs ", lvls[1], " (Baseline)")

# Extract results safely
spicy_df <- as.data.frame(spicyR::topPairs(spicy_results, n = Inf))
spicy_df$cell_pair <- paste(spicy_df$from, spicy_df$to, sep = " → ")

message("\nTop 10 most SIGNIFICANT pairs (by p-value):")
print(head(spicy_df[order(spicy_df$p.value), c("cell_pair", "coefficient", "p.value")], 10))

message("\nTop 10 most POSITIVE differences (Higher colocalization in ", lvls[2], "):")
print(head(spicy_df[order(spicy_df$coefficient, decreasing = TRUE), c("cell_pair", "coefficient", "p.value")], 10))

message("\nTop 10 most NEGATIVE differences (Higher colocalization in ", lvls[1], "):")
print(head(spicy_df[order(spicy_df$coefficient), c("cell_pair", "coefficient", "p.value")], 10))

# Summary of significant results
# Using p.value (raw) and coefficient
sig_count <- sum(spicy_df$p.value < 0.05)
pos_sig <- sum(spicy_df$p.value < 0.05 & spicy_df$coefficient > 0)
neg_sig <- sum(spicy_df$p.value < 0.05 & spicy_df$coefficient < 0)

message("\nSummary of results with p < 0.05:")
message("  Total significant pairs: ", sig_count)
message("  Significant attraction in ", lvls[2], " (RED): ", pos_sig)
message("  Significant attraction in ", lvls[1], " (BLUE): ", neg_sig)
```

### 5.10.4 Absolute Colocalization Heatmaps

The `signifPlot` above only shows **differences** between conditions. To see absolute **attraction** (where cells are physically closer than random), we can plot the raw L-function values for each condition separately.

``` {r absolute_colocalisation_heatmaps, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Load the per-image stats
coloc_data <- read.csv(file.path(coloc_dir, "colocalisation_per_image.csv"))

# Average by condition
coloc_summary <- coloc_data %>%
  # Extract condition from imageID (assuming CAR/EGFR prefix)
  mutate(condition = ifelse(grepl("CAR", imageID), "CAR", "EGFR")) %>%
  group_by(condition, from_cellType, to_cellType) %>%
  summarise(mean_L = mean(L_function, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Plot Heatmap for each condition
p <- ggplot(coloc_summary, aes(x = from_cellType, y = to_cellType, fill = mean_L)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~condition) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Absolute Colocalization (L-function)",
    subtitle = "Red = Attraction (Closer than random), Blue = Avoidance (Further than random)",
    fill = "L-Value"
  )

print(p)

# Save heatmap
heatmap_file <- file.path(coloc_dir, "absolute_colocalisation_heatmap.png")
ggsave(heatmap_file, p, width = 12, height = 8)
message("✓ Absolute colocalization heatmap saved to: ", basename(heatmap_file))

# List top Attraction pairs (L > 0)
attraction_pairs <- coloc_summary %>%
  filter(mean_L > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_L))

message("\nTop Absolute Attraction Pairs across both conditions:")
print(head(attraction_pairs, 20))
```

# 6. Cell Relationships Relative to Expected Behaviour (Kontextual)

Understanding spatial relationships between cell types is essential for interpreting how cells function within their native tissue environments. Yet, these relationships can be influenced by confounding factors like uneven cell distributions, tissue architecture, and the specific regions imaged. The **Kontextual** method, available in the **Statial** package, tackles these challenges by integrating biological context directly into spatial analysis.

Instead of assessing cell positions in isolation, Kontextual defines reference contexts—such as local neighbourhood composition or tissue compartments—and evaluates whether particular cell types are clustered or dispersed within these settings. This strategy reduces the impact of structural inhomogeneity and sampling bias, enabling more robust, biologically meaningful insights into spatial organisation.

In this section, we demonstrate how to use Statial to extract contextualised spatial metrics and interpret localisation patterns with greater confidence.

## 6.0 Optional: Load Data from Previous Section

If you've already completed Section 5 and want to resume from here, you can load the saved data object.

``` {r load_section5_data, eval=FALSE}
# Uncomment and run this chunk to load data from end of Section 5
# checkpoint_dir <- file.path(PROG_DIR, "Checkpoints")

# message("✓ Loaded data from end of Section 5")
```

## 6.1 Define Cell Type Hierarchies

A cell type hierarchy defines how cell types are functionally related to one another. The bottom of the hierarchy represents homogeneous populations (children), and nodes represent broader parent populations with shared function.

``` {r define_hierarchies}
message("Defining cell type hierarchies...")

# Examine all cell types (clusters)
all_cell_types <- unique(combined_spe$cellType)
message("\nCell types in dataset: ", length(all_cell_types))
message("  ", paste(sort(all_cell_types), collapse = ", "))

# Define biological hierarchy based on spleen germinal center architecture
# This reflects the expected tissue compartments and lineages
biologicalHierarchy <- list()

# ===== MAJOR LINEAGES =====

# B Cell Lineage (Germinal Center and Activated)
biologicalHierarchy$B_cells <- c(
  "Germinal Center B cells",
  "Activated B cells"
)

# T Cell Lineage (All T cell subsets)
biologicalHierarchy$T_cells <- c(
  "Regulatory T cells (Tregs)",
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs",
  "Follicular Helper T (Tfh)",
  "Tfh/Cytotoxic cells",
  "CD8+ Effector T cells",
  "Activated Memory T cells",
  "Th2-like cells",
  "Pro-inflammatory T/ILC",
  "Resting/Naive Lymphocytes"
)

# Myeloid/Antigen Presenting Cells
biologicalHierarchy$Myeloid_APC <- c(
  "Myeloid/APC"
)

# ===== T CELL SUBSETS =====

# Regulatory T cells (FoxP3+ enriched)
biologicalHierarchy$Regulatory_T_cells <- c(
  "Regulatory T cells (Tregs)",
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs"
)

# Helper T cells (CD4+ subsets)
biologicalHierarchy$Helper_T_cells <- c(
  "Follicular Helper T (Tfh)",
  "Tfh/Cytotoxic cells",
  "Th2-like cells",
  "Activated Memory T cells"
)

# Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+ and GranzB+)
biologicalHierarchy$Cytotoxic_T_cells <- c(
  "CD8+ Effector T cells",
  "Tfh/Cytotoxic cells",
  "Granzyme A+ cytotoxic"
)

# Activated T cells (high activation markers)
biologicalHierarchy$Activated_T_cells <- c(
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs",
  "Activated Memory T cells",
  "Highly Activated cells",
  "Pro-inflammatory T/ILC"
)

# Resting/Naive cells
biologicalHierarchy$Resting_cells <- c(
  "Resting/Naive Lymphocytes"
)

# ===== FUNCTIONAL GROUPS =====

# Germinal Center-associated cells (GC B cells + Tfh)
biologicalHierarchy$Germinal_Center <- c(
  "Germinal Center B cells",
  "Follicular Helper T (Tfh)",
  "Tfh/Cytotoxic cells"
)

# T Zone cells (non-GC T cells and APCs)
biologicalHierarchy$T_Zone <- c(
  "Regulatory T cells (Tregs)",
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs",
  "CD8+ Effector T cells",
  "Activated Memory T cells",
  "Pro-inflammatory T/ILC",
  "Myeloid/APC"
)

# Highly activated/effector cells (strong activation signatures)
biologicalHierarchy$Highly_Activated <- c(
  "Highly Activated cells",
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs",
  "Granzyme A+ cytotoxic",
  "Pro-inflammatory T/ILC"
)

# ===== FOXP3+ GROUPS (PRIMARY RESEARCH QUESTION) =====

# FoxP3+ enriched cell types (from Section 5.8 analysis)
biologicalHierarchy$FoxP3_enriched <- c(
  "Germinal Center B cells", # Highest FoxP3 expression
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs", # True Tregs
  "GFP+ cells (CAR-T?)", # GFP+ CAR-T cells
  "Regulatory T cells (Tregs)" # Classical Tregs
)

# True regulatory T cells (Treg subsets)
biologicalHierarchy$True_Tregs <- c(
  "Regulatory T cells (Tregs)",
  "GFP+ Activated Tregs"
)

# ===== SPATIAL COMPARTMENTS =====

# All immune cells (entire dataset)
biologicalHierarchy$All_Immune <- all_cell_types

# Print hierarchy structure
message("\n✓ Hierarchy defined based on spleen germinal center biology")
message("\nHierarchy levels:")
message(
  "  1. Major Lineages: B_cells (n=", length(biologicalHierarchy$B_cells),
  "), T_cells (n=", length(biologicalHierarchy$T_cells),
  "), Myeloid_APC (n=", length(biologicalHierarchy$Myeloid_APC), ")"
)
message("  2. T Cell Subsets: Regulatory, Helper, Cytotoxic, Activated, Resting")
message("  3. Functional Groups: Germinal_Center, T_Zone, Highly_Activated")
message("  4. FoxP3 Groups: FoxP3_enriched, True_Tregs (PRIMARY RESEARCH QUESTION)")

message("\n🎯 Key Contexts for Analysis:")
message("  - Germinal_Center: GC B cells and Tfh (follicular niche)")
message("  - T_Zone: Tregs, effector T, APC (T zone/mantle)")
message("  - True_Tregs: Regulatory T cell subsets (FoxP3+ focus)")
```

> **Important**: Before running Kontextual analysis, you should:
> 1. Review your cluster marker heatmap (Section 4.6)
> 2. Annotate clusters with meaningful cell type names
> 3. Define biologically relevant parent-child relationships

## 6.3 Example: Visualize Cell Types in Context

Let's visualize the spatial distribution of selected cell types to understand potential context-dependent relationships.

``` {r visualize_context, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
# Select a few clusters to visualize
```

## 6.4 Calculate Kontextual Metrics for Multiple Pairs

We'll calculate Kontextual metrics for multiple cell type pairs across both images to systematically compare context-dependent relationships.

``` {r calculate_kontextual_multiple}
message("Calculating Kontextual metrics for top cell type pairs...")
message("Note: With only 2 images, statistical testing is limited")

# Initialize results storage
kontextual_results_list <- list()
kontextual_summary <- data.frame()

# Select top pairs from spicyR analysis (Section 5) to focus on
if (exists("lfunction_summary")) {
  # Get top 10 most significant pairs from Section 5
  top_pairs_for_kontext <- head(lfunction_summary %>% arrange(desc(abs(mean_L))), 10)
  pairs_to_test <- top_pairs_for_kontext$cell_pair

  message("\nTesting Kontextual for top ", length(pairs_to_test), " cell type pairs from spicyR results")
} else {
  # Fallback: test first few pairs
  # Get all cell types if missing
  if (!exists("all_cell_types")) all_cell_types <- unique(combined_spe$cellType)

  if (length(all_cell_types) >= 2) {
    pairs_to_test <- c(paste0(all_cell_types[1], "__", all_cell_types[2]))
    message("\n⚠️  spicyR results not found, testing limited pairs")
  } else {
    pairs_to_test <- character(0)
    message("\n⚠️  Need at least 2 cell types for analysis")
  }
}

# Calculate Kontextual for each pair
if (length(pairs_to_test) > 0) {
  for (i in seq_along(pairs_to_test)) {
    pair <- pairs_to_test[i]
    parts <- strsplit(pair, "__")[[1]]

    if (length(parts) == 2) {
      from_type <- parts[1]
      to_type <- parts[2]

      # Define parent context (use all cell types for now)
      # TODO: Update this with your biologically meaningful hierarchy
      parent_context <- all_cell_types

      message("\n[", i, "/", length(pairs_to_test), "] ", from_type, " → ", to_type)

      # Calculate Kontextual
      kontext_result <- tryCatch(
        {
          Statial::Kontextual(
            cells = combined_spe,
            r = 100, # Radius in pixels
            from = from_type,
            to = to_type,
            parent = parent_context,
            cellType = "cellType",
            imageID = "imageID"
          )
        },
        error = function(e) {
          message("  ⚠️  Error: ", e$message)
          return(NULL)
        }
      )

      if (!is.null(kontext_result)) {
        # Store results
        kontext_df <- as.data.frame(kontext_result)
        kontext_df$from_cellType <- from_type
        kontext_df$to_cellType <- to_type
        kontext_df$cell_pair <- pair

        kontextual_summary <- rbind(kontextual_summary, kontext_df)
        kontextual_results_list[[pair]] <- kontext_df

        message("  ✓ Complete")
      }
    }
  }

  message("\n✓ Kontextual calculation complete for ", nrow(kontextual_summary), " relationships")
} else {
  message("\n⚠️  No pairs to test")
}
```

## 6.4.1 Compare Kontextual Results Between Images

With 2 images, we can compare how context-dependent relationships differ between them.

``` {r compare_kontextual_between_images, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}
if (nrow(kontextual_summary) > 0) {
  message("\nComparing Kontextual results between images...")

  # Calculate difference in kontextual metric between images
  kontextual_comparison <- kontextual_summary %>%
    group_by(cell_pair, from_cellType, to_cellType) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_original = mean(original, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_kontextual = mean(kontextual, na.rm = TRUE),
      diff_original = diff(original),
      diff_kontextual = diff(kontextual),
      context_effect = mean_kontextual - mean_original,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(diff_kontextual)))

  message("\nTop 10 pairs with largest Kontextual differences between images:")
  print(head(kontextual_comparison, 10))

  # Export full results
  kontext_export <- file.path(kontextual_dir, "kontextual_all_pairs.csv")
  write.csv(kontextual_summary, kontext_export, row.names = FALSE)
  message("\n✓ Full Kontextual results saved to: ", basename(kontext_export))

  # Export comparison
  kontext_comp_file <- file.path(kontextual_dir, "kontextual_comparison_between_images.csv")
  write.csv(kontextual_comparison, kontext_comp_file, row.names = FALSE)
  message("✓ Kontextual comparison saved to: ", basename(kontext_comp_file))

  # Visualize: Compare original vs kontextual for top pairs
  top_6_pairs <- head(kontextual_comparison, 6)

  if (nrow(top_6_pairs) > 0) {
    plot_data <- kontextual_summary %>%
      filter(cell_pair %in% top_6_pairs$cell_pair) %>%
      pivot_longer(
        cols = c(original, kontextual),
        names_to = "metric_type",
        values_to = "value"
      )

    comparison_plot <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = cell_pair, y = value, fill = metric_type)) +
      geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
      facet_wrap(~imageID, ncol = 1) +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(
        title = "Original vs Kontextual L-function: Top 6 Pairs",
        subtitle = "Difference between metrics indicates context-dependent relationships",
        x = "Cell Type Pair",
        y = "L-function Value",
        fill = "Metric"
      ) +
      theme_classic() +
      theme(
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top"
      ) +
      scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("original" = "steelblue", "kontextual" = "coral"),
        labels = c("original" = "Original (spicyR)", "kontextual" = "Kontextual (context-aware)")
      )

    print(comparison_plot)

    # Save
    comp_plot_file <- file.path(kontextual_dir, "kontextual_vs_original_comparison.png")
    ggsave(comp_plot_file, plot = comparison_plot, width = 14, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
    message("✓ Comparison plot saved to: ", basename(comp_plot_file))
  }

  # Identify context-dependent pairs (where sign changes or magnitude changes significantly)
  context_dependent <- kontextual_comparison %>%
    mutate(
      sign_change = sign(mean_original) != sign(mean_kontextual),
      magnitude_change = abs(context_effect) > abs(mean_original) * 0.3
    ) %>%
    filter(sign_change | magnitude_change) %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(context_effect)))

  if (nrow(context_dependent) > 0) {
    message("\n📍 Context-dependent relationships detected:")
    message("  ", nrow(context_dependent), " pairs show significant context effects")
    message("\nTop 5 context-dependent pairs:")
    for (i in 1:min(5, nrow(context_dependent))) {
      pair <- context_dependent$cell_pair[i]
      orig <- round(context_dependent$mean_original[i], 2)
      kont <- round(context_dependent$mean_kontextual[i], 2)
      change <- ifelse(context_dependent$sign_change[i], "SIGN CHANGE", "magnitude shift")
      message("  ", i, ". ", pair, ": ", orig, " → ", kont, " (", change, ")")
    }

    # Export context-dependent pairs
    context_dep_file <- file.path(kontextual_dir, "kontextual_context_dependent_pairs.csv")
    write.csv(context_dependent, context_dep_file, row.names = FALSE)
    message("\n✓ Context-dependent pairs saved to: ", basename(context_dep_file))
  } else {
    message("\n  No strong context-dependent relationships detected")
  }
} else {
  message("\n⚠️  No Kontextual results to compare")
}
```

## 6.5 Kontextual Curve (Range of Radii)

The `kontextCurve` function evaluates spatial relationships across multiple radii, showing how context affects interpretation at different spatial scales.

``` {r kontextual_curve, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(kontextual_summary) > 0) {
  message("Calculating Kontextual curves for top 2 pairs across multiple radii...")
  message("  Testing radii: 50, 100, 150, 200 pixels")

  # Select top 2 pairs with largest context effects
  if (exists("kontextual_comparison")) {
    top_2_for_curves <- head(kontextual_comparison, 2)
  } else {
    top_2_for_curves <- head(kontextual_summary, 2)
  }

  curve_plots <- list()

  if (!exists("all_cell_types")) all_cell_types <- unique(combined_spe$cellType)
  for (i in 1:min(2, nrow(top_2_for_curves))) {
    if ("cell_pair" %in% colnames(top_2_for_curves)) {
      pair <- top_2_for_curves$cell_pair[i]
      parts <- strsplit(pair, "__")[[1]]
      from_type <- parts[1]
      to_type <- parts[2]
    } else {
      from_type <- top_2_for_curves$from_cellType[i]
      to_type <- top_2_for_curves$to_cellType[i]
    }

    # Calculate for both images
    for (img_id in unique(combined_spe$imageID)) {
      message("\n  Calculating curve: ", from_type, " → ", to_type, " (", img_id, ")")

      kontextual_curve <- tryCatch(
        {
          Statial::kontextCurve(
            cells = combined_spe,
            from = from_type,
            to = to_type,
            parent = all_cell_types, # Use all cell types as parent
            rs = seq(50, 200, 50),
            image = img_id,
            cellType = "cellType",
            imageID = "imageID"
          )
        },
        error = function(e) {
          message("    ⚠️  Error: ", e$message)
          return(NULL)
        }
      )

      if (!is.null(kontextual_curve)) {
        # Plot the curve
        p <- Statial::kontextPlot(kontextual_curve) +
          labs(
            title = paste0(from_type, " → ", to_type),
            subtitle = paste0("Image: ", img_id)
          ) +
          theme_classic()

        curve_plots[[paste0(from_type, "__", to_type, "__", img_id)]] <- p
      }
    }
  }

  # Display curves
  if (length(curve_plots) > 0) {
    gridExtra::grid.arrange(grobs = curve_plots, ncol = 2)

    # Save
    curves_file <- file.path(kontextual_dir, "kontextual_curves_top_pairs.png")
    ggsave(
      filename = curves_file,
      plot = gridExtra::arrangeGrob(grobs = curve_plots, ncol = 2),
      width = 14,
      height = 6 * ceiling(length(curve_plots) / 2),
      dpi = 300,
      bg = "white"
    )

    message("\n✓ Kontextual curves saved to: ", basename(curves_file))

    message("\nInterpretation:")
    message("  - Points ABOVE red line = localization at that radius")
    message("  - Points BELOW red line = dispersion at that radius")
    message("  - Blue (original) vs Orange (kontextual) shows context impact")
  }
} else {
  message("\n⚠️  No Kontextual results available for curve analysis")
}
```

# 7. Identifying Spatial Domains with Unsupervised Clustering

Beyond pairwise spatial relationships between cell types, imaging datasets reveal richer layers of tissue organisation through concepts like **niches**, **neighborhoods**, **microenvironments**, and **spatial domains**. Niches typically describe the immediate surroundings of a specific cell, while spatial domains represent larger tissue compartments formed by coordinated cell arrangements.

The **lisaClust** package identifies spatial domains by clustering cells based on their local spatial association patterns. This method groups tissue regions with similar spatial signatures, uncovering emergent domains within complex tissue landscapes.

## 7.2 Set Expected Spatial Structures (Spleen Tissue)

For spleen tissue sections, we expect specific microanatomical structures:

**Expected Structures:**
1. **Germinal Centers (GC)**: PNA+ core regions (B cell proliferation centers)
2. **Follicle Mantle Zones**: CD19+ B cell-rich regions flanking GCs
3. **T cell Zones**: CD4+ T cell-rich regions adjacent to follicles
4. **IA-IE+ Follicular Regions**: Antigen-presenting cell-rich zones
5. **Interfollicular/Red Pulp**: Mixed populations outside organized lymphoid structures

``` {r define_spleen_structures}
message("Setting up lisaClust for spleen tissue microanatomy...")

# Expected number of spatial domains based on spleen structure
# GC core, Mantle zone, T zone, Interfollicular, Background = 5 domains minimum
# May need 6-8 to capture sub-compartments (e.g., light vs dark zone GC)
k_regions <- 8 # Increased to resolve distinct Tfh zone and Treg-enriched zone

message("\n🧬 Spleen Tissue Expected Structures:")
message("  1. Germinal Centers (PNA+)")
message("  2. Follicle Mantle Zones (CD19+)")
message("  3. T Cell Zones (CD4+)")
message("  4. IA-IE+ Follicular Regions (APC-rich)")
message("  5. Interfollicular/Red Pulp")
message("  6. Transitional/Mixed Zones")

message("\n📊 Dataset Summary:")
message("  Number of spatial domains (k): ", k_regions)
message("  Cell types: ", length(unique(combined_spe$cellType)))
message("  Images: ", length(unique(combined_spe$imageID)))
message("  Total cells: ", format(ncol(combined_spe), big.mark = ","))
```

## 7.3 Run lisaClust to Identify Spatial Domains

`lisaClust` uses local indicators of spatial association (LISA) to identify regions where specific cell types co-localize. For each cell, it calculates how strongly it is surrounded by other cell types relative to what would be expected by chance.

``` {r identify_spatial_domains}
message("\nRunning lisaClust to identify spatial domains...")

# Run lisaClust to identify spatial domains
# Radii chosen to capture:
#   - 20 pixels: immediate cellular neighborhoods
#   - 50 pixels: local domain structure
#   - 100 pixels: larger compartments (follicles, T zones)
combined_spe <- lisaClust::lisaClust(
  combined_spe,
  k = k_regions,
  Rs = c(20, 50, 100), # Multi-scale analysis
  sigma = 50, # Smoothing for spatial continuity
  spatialCoords = c("x", "y"),
  cellType = "cellType",
  imageID = "imageID",
  BPPARAM = BPPARAM
)

message("\n✓ Spatial domains identified")

# Examine the regions
regions_summary <- table(
  Image = colData(combined_spe)$imageID,
  Region = colData(combined_spe)$region
)

message("\nRegion distribution across images:")
print(regions_summary)

# Overall region counts
message("\nTotal cells per region:")
region_counts <- table(combined_spe$region)
print(region_counts)

# Calculate region sizes (as % of total)
region_pct <- round(100 * region_counts / sum(region_counts), 1)
message("\nRegion sizes (% of total cells):")
for (i in seq_along(region_pct)) {
  message("  ", names(region_pct)[i], ": ", region_pct[i], "%")
}

# Define consistent colors for regions
# We use a palette that can handle up to 10-12 regions
region_pal <- c(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Set2"), RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Accent"))
region_cols <- region_pal[1:k_regions]
names(region_cols) <- paste0("region_", 1:k_regions)

message("\nDefined consistent colors for ", k_regions, " regions.")
```

> **What is k?** The number of spatial domains to identify. For spleen:
> - Start with k=6 (GC, Mantle, T zone, Follicular, Interfollicular, Mixed)
> - Increase to k=8-10 if you want to distinguish GC light/dark zones or T cell subregions
> - Decrease to k=4-5 for coarser compartments

## 7.3.5 Examine Cell Type Enrichment in Each Region

The `regionMap` function shows which cell types are enriched in each spatial domain.

``` {r region_cell_type_enrichment, fig.width=16, fig.height=8}
message("Analyzing cell type enrichment in spatial domains...")

# Get unique image IDs
image_ids <- unique(combined_spe$imageID)

# 1. Calculate enrichment data per image
# We loop through each image, run regionMap, and extract the data slot
# from the returned ggplot object.
region_data_list <- lapply(image_ids, function(id) {
  message("  Processing image: ", id)
  spe_sub <- combined_spe[, combined_spe$imageID == id]

  # Run regionMap
  p <- lisaClust::regionMap(spe_sub, type = "bubble")
  df <- p$data

  # DIAGNOSTIC: Print columns to console
  message("    Columns found: ", paste(colnames(df), collapse = ", "))
  # print(head(df))

  # Harmonize Region column
  if ("Region" %in% colnames(df)) colnames(df)[colnames(df) == "Region"] <- "region"

  # Harmonize Cell Type column
  if ("CT" %in% colnames(df)) colnames(df)[colnames(df) == "CT"] <- "cellType"

  # Harmonize Count column
  if ("Freq" %in% colnames(df)) colnames(df)[colnames(df) == "Freq"] <- "count"

  # Harmonize Enrichment column
  # Priority: enrichment, value, score, log2FC
  if (!"enrichment" %in% colnames(df)) {
    candidates <- c("value", "score", "log2FC", "Enrichment")
    found <- FALSE
    for (col in candidates) {
      if (col %in% colnames(df)) {
        colnames(df)[colnames(df) == col] <- "enrichment"
        found <- TRUE
        break
      }
    }

    # If still not found, take the numeric column that hasn't been named yet
    if (!found) {
      num_cols <- names(df)[sapply(df, is.numeric)]
      rem_cols <- setdiff(num_cols, c("region", "cellType", "count"))
      if (length(rem_cols) > 0) {
        message("    Using '", rem_cols[1], "' as enrichment column")
        colnames(df)[colnames(df) == rem_cols[1]] <- "enrichment"
      }
    }
  }

  df$imageID <- id
  return(df)
})

# Combine all images into one data frame
region_data_combined <- do.call(rbind, region_data_list)

# 2. Create Faceted Bubble Plot
# We use ggplot2 directly to ensure the imageID variable is available for faceting
# We use the column names we ensured above
region_bubble <- ggplot(region_data_combined, aes(x = region, y = cellType, size = count, color = enrichment)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~imageID) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Cell Type Enrichment by Spatial Domain",
    subtitle = "Faceted by Image | Bubble size = cells | Color = enrichment (obs/exp)",
    x = "Spatial Domain",
    y = "Cell Type",
    size = "Cell Count",
    color = "Enrichment"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray95"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

print(region_bubble)

# Save Bubble Plot
bubble_file <- file.path(domains_dir, "spatial_domains_bubble_faceted.png")
ggsave(
  filename = bubble_file,
  plot = region_bubble,
  width = 18,
  height = 8,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)
message("✓ Bubble plot saved to: ", basename(bubble_file))

# 3. Create Faceted Heatmap Plot
region_heatmap <- ggplot(region_data_combined, aes(x = region, y = cellType, fill = enrichment)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~imageID) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Cell Type Composition by Spatial Domain",
    subtitle = "Faceted by Image | Color intensity = enrichment score",
    x = "Spatial Domain",
    y = "Cell Type",
    fill = "Enrichment"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray95"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

print(region_heatmap)

# Save Heatmap Plot
heatmap_file <- file.path(domains_dir, "spatial_domains_heatmap_faceted.png")
ggsave(
  filename = heatmap_file,
  plot = region_heatmap,
  width = 16,
  height = 8,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)
message("✓ Heatmap saved to: ", basename(heatmap_file))
```

**Interpretation**:
- **Large bubbles**: Many cells of that type
- **Red/warm colors**: Cell type is MORE abundant than expected (enriched)
- **Blue/cool colors**: Cell type is LESS abundant than expected (depleted)

## 7.4 Visualize Spatial Domains on Tissue

The `hatchingPlot` function visualizes spatial domains overlaid on the tissue, with different hatching patterns for each region.

``` {r visualize_spatial_domains, fig.width=14, fig.height=7}
message("Visualizing spatial domains on tissue...")

# Create hatching plots for both images
hatching_plots <- list()

for (img_id in unique(combined_spe$imageID)) {
  message("  Creating hatching plot for image: ", img_id)

  # Generate hatching plot
  p <- tryCatch(
    {
      lisaClust::hatchingPlot(
        combined_spe,
        useImages = img_id,
        nbp = 100, # Grid resolution for hatching (reduced from 300 to avoid timeout)
        hatching.colour = "black"
      ) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Spatial Domains:", img_id),
          subtitle = "Hatching patterns = regions | Colors = cell types"
        ) +
        theme_classic() +
        theme(legend.position = "right")
    },
    error = function(e) {
      message("    ⚠️  Error creating hatching plot: ", e$message)
      message("    Creating simplified spatial plot instead...")

      # Fallback: simple spatial plot
      img_data <- cbind(
        as.data.frame(spatialCoords(combined_spe)),
        as.data.frame(colData(combined_spe))
      ) %>%
        filter(imageID == img_id)

      ggplot(img_data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = region)) +
        geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
        scale_color_manual(values = region_cols) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Spatial Domains:", img_id),
          subtitle = "Colors = spatial domains",
          color = "Region"
        ) +
        theme_classic()
    }
  )

  hatching_plots[[img_id]] <- p
}

# Display side-by-side
gridExtra::grid.arrange(grobs = hatching_plots, ncol = 2)

# Save
hatching_file <- file.path(domains_dir, "spatial_domains_hatching.png")
ggsave(
  filename = hatching_file,
  plot = gridExtra::arrangeGrob(grobs = hatching_plots, ncol = 2),
  width = 14,
  height = 7,
  dpi = 150,
  bg = "white"
)

message("✓ Hatching plots saved to: ", basename(hatching_file))
```
